clue.text: The Loneliness of the Outside Left

definitions.text: The Loneliness of the Outside Left

blocks.clueFragment: The Loneliness of the Outside Left
blocks.note: surface reading: a spoof of the film title The Loneliness of the Long Distance Runner, about a footballer on the left wing
setter's reading: the state of being left outside on your own, which is loneliness itself

explanation.surface: A film or novel title about the lonely life of a left-winger in football.
explanation.walkthrough: An outside left is a winger in old football formations; read literally, someone left outside alone is in a state of isolation.
explanation.definitionFit: Solitude is the condition of being alone, a close synonym for loneliness.

clue.text: Greek warrior provides a vote for German 10

blocks.note: taken as written
ja is German for yes, the vote in favour
X is ten in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: A Greek hero is pictured backing a German candidate, with a cross-reference to another clue.
explanation.walkthrough: The 10 looks like a cross-reference to 10 across, but it simply stands for the Roman numeral.
explanation.definitionFit: Ajax was a mighty hero who fought for the Greeks at Troy in Homer's Iliad.

clue.text: Determined to exclude religious education from the web?

indicators.note: excluding something means leaving it out, so letters are dropped from the word for the web

blocks.note: RE is the school subject abbreviation
the web is the internet

explanation.surface: Someone set on keeping religious teaching off the internet.
explanation.walkthrough: Taking RE out of INTERNET leaves INTENT.
explanation.definitionFit: Being intent on something means being resolved or set upon doing it.

clue.text: Dialect that comes from the mouth

blocks.note: first meaning: ... English, the accent of south-east England around the Thames
second meaning: the wide tidal mouth of a river

explanation.surface: A remark that speech, of whatever accent, comes out of the mouth.
explanation.walkthrough: Estuary English is a British accent named after the Thames estuary; 'mouth' here is a river's, not a person's.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both a regional British speech variety and the broad tidal outlet where a river meets the sea.

clue.text: Pay it and sod off to Brave New World, say

indicators.note: something gone off is spoiled or out of its proper state, so these letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A rude dismissal: pay up and clear off to the world of Huxley's novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sod off' reads as a rude phrase, but 'off' alone is the anagram signal and 'sod' is fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Huxley's Brave New World is a classic example of a nightmarish imagined society.

clue.text: Absolutely wet?

blocks.note: first meaning: an emphatic exclamation of agreement
second meaning: a wet is a moderate Conservative, only somewhat right-wing

explanation.walkthrough: In British politics a wet was a moderate Tory under Thatcher, so read as two words the answer describes someone moderately right-wing.
explanation.definitionFit: As an exclamation it means 'I agree entirely'; read literally it means fairly right-wing, as a moderate Tory is.

clue.text: Don't look at topless women in Rimini!

indicators.note: without a top, so the first letter is removed from the Italian word

blocks.note: signore is Italian for ladies, plural of signora; Rimini is an Italian resort

explanation.surface: A warning to avert one's eyes from topless sunbathers on an Italian beach.
explanation.walkthrough: SIGNORE without its first letter gives IGNORE.
explanation.definitionFit: To ignore something is to pay it no attention, to deliberately not look at it.

clue.text: Books about Joyce's first working title

indicators.note: only the opening letter of the writer's name is taken
about means going round, so the books wrap around what follows

blocks.note: tomes are large books
the initial of Joyce
a machine that is working is on

explanation.surface: A note on books about James Joyce and the provisional title of his work.
explanation.walkthrough: Tom Jones is Henry Fielding's novel. 'Working title' tempts as one phrase, but 'working' stands alone for a machine that is running.
explanation.definitionFit: Tom Jones is the title of Henry Fielding's eighteenth-century comic novel.

clue.text: Litter no guy disturbed

indicators.note: disturbed things are thrown out of order, so these letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A tidy man who would not be bothered by rubbish lying about.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Litter' looks like rubbish but means a brood of animal offspring.
explanation.definitionFit: A litter is the offspring born to an animal at one time, its young.

clue.text: Unpredictable woman's formula includes nitrogen

indicators.note: something that includes another holds it inside, so the gas goes within the formula

blocks.note: a mix is a formula of ingredients
N is the chemical symbol for nitrogen

explanation.surface: A chemist's remark that a capricious woman's recipe contains nitrogen.
explanation.definitionFit: A minx is a cheeky, wilful and capricious young woman.

clue.text: Victoria perhaps beheaded after rejecting cure for wind

indicators.note: rejecting suggests throwing back, so the word for a remedy is read backwards
a beheaded word loses its first letters, its head

blocks.note: taken as written
Victoria is a London railway station

explanation.surface: Queen Victoria executed after turning down a remedy for flatulence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Victoria' suggests the queen, but it is the London station; beheaded drops its first two letters, S and T, leaving TATION.
explanation.definitionFit: Eructation is the formal term for belching, expelling gas from the stomach.

clue.text: Strike for unlimited food

blocks.note: first meaning: to batter or knock about, as waves do
second meaning: a meal where diners help themselves to as much as they like

explanation.surface: Workers walking out in protest to demand free meals.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is a verb for hitting repeatedly and a noun for a self-service spread of dishes.

clue.text: Film script's material turning on iron weapon

indicators.note: turning round means the material for the script is read backwards

blocks.note: a flick is an informal word for a film
handwriting is done in ink
Fe is the chemical symbol for iron

explanation.surface: A film screenplay whose material switches on an iron weapon.
explanation.definitionFit: A flick knife is a knife whose blade springs out at the press of a button, a weapon.

clue.text: Journalist's banger

blocks.note: first meaning: a news writer
second meaning: something that makes a report, a loud bang, like a firework

explanation.walkthrough: A banger is British slang for a sausage or an old car, but here it is a firework, and a report is the sound of an explosion.
explanation.definitionFit: A newspaper writer files reports; read whimsically, anything that gives off a loud report, a bang, is one too.

clue.text: Steady return covering unhealthy man

indicators.note: a return goes back the way it came, so the word for steady is read backwards
covering means wrapping round, so the reversed word encloses the next piece

blocks.note: steady and even both mean regular
unhealthy means ill

explanation.surface: A steady return home for a man who is unwell.
explanation.definitionFit: Neville is a man's first name, so a man is a fair crossword-style general definition.

clue.text: Superlatively dizzy, dishes in the dosh

indicators.note: in places one thing inside another, so the dishes go within the money

blocks.note: dosh and loot are both slang for money
pies are dishes

explanation.surface: A giddy person rolling in money, lining up their plates.
explanation.walkthrough: Dosh is British slang for cash.
explanation.definitionFit: Loopy means crazy or giddy, and the -est ending makes it superlative.

clue.text: Jocular desire to admit a horse, say

indicators.note: admitting someone lets them in, so the wish takes the horse inside it

blocks.note: a wish is a desire
taken as written
gee-gee is a child's word for a horse

explanation.surface: A playful longing to let a horse into the house.
explanation.walkthrough: Gee-gee is nursery talk for a horse, and 'say' flags that it is an informal example.
explanation.definitionFit: Waggish describes a humorous, playfully mischievous manner, much like jocular.

clue.text: Code-breaking in stately home's inner shell

indicators.note: a code being broken is taken apart, so its letters are rearranged
in places the jumbled letters inside the home

blocks.note: taken as written
a seat is a country house, the family seat

explanation.surface: Codebreakers at work inside a grand country house, like Bletchley Park.
explanation.walkthrough: A seat is the main residence of an aristocratic family, so 'stately home' is a fair hint.
explanation.definitionFit: A seed coat is the protective outer layer around a plant's embryo, the shell within the fruit.

clue.text: Laurel's wreathing South Africa's poetry

indicators.note: a wreath encircles something, so the comedian's name wraps around the country

blocks.note: Stan Laurel of Laurel and Hardy, plus the S of the possessive
ZA is the international code for South Africa

explanation.surface: A laurel wreath placed on the poetry of South Africa, as an honour for a poet.
explanation.walkthrough: Laurel suggests a poet's crown, but it is the comedian Stan Laurel.
explanation.definitionFit: Stanzas are the verses or groups of lines that make up a poem, so they are poetry.

clue.text: Case of the second date

blocks.note: to second is to back or support, as a stake supports a plant
a date is an outing, going out together

explanation.surface: A romantic second date discussed as if it were a detective's case.
explanation.walkthrough: To case a place is to watch it before a crime, which a stakeout does.
explanation.definitionFit: Casing a joint and a stakeout both mean keeping a place under covert surveillance.

clue.text: Artist featuring in current polemical outburst

indicators.note: featuring in means appearing within, so the artist sits inside the current

blocks.note: a tide is a current of water
RA is a Royal Academician

explanation.surface: A painter caught up in a heated public rant.
explanation.definitionFit: A tirade is a long angry speech of denunciation, an impassioned outburst.

clue.text: Noble bird went ahead

blocks.note: a tit is a small songbird
to go ahead is to lead

explanation.surface: A grand bird striding out in front of the flock.
explanation.definitionFit: A titled person holds a rank in the aristocracy, a lord or lady.

clue.text: Woman volunteers to take control

indicators.note: taking something in means holding it, so the volunteers enclose the control

blocks.note: the TA, Territorial Army, was Britain's volunteer reserve
at the helm means in control

explanation.surface: A woman stepping up to command a group of volunteers.
explanation.definitionFit: Thelma is a female first name, so a woman is a general crossword definition.

clue.text: Bridge team that's in switched-off state - it can't last

indicators.note: in places the bridge pair and the 'that is' inside the switched-off state

blocks.note: a trance is a dazed state where the mind is switched off
North and South form one partnership at bridge
i.e. is the abbreviation of id est, that is

explanation.surface: A bridge team in a trance, with a warning that this cannot go on.
explanation.walkthrough: At bridge the four players are named by compass points, and North and South play as partners.
explanation.definitionFit: Transience is the quality of being temporary, of something that is fleeting and soon passes.

clue.text: Stick up for bird

blocks.note: first meaning: to raise or turn upward, as a dog does its ears
second meaning: a male fowl

explanation.surface: An appeal to defend a bird.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stick up for' reads as defend, but 'for' is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To cock something is to tilt it upward, and a cock is a male chicken or other bird.

clue.text: Man upended to produce glazed effect

indicators.note: upended means turned upside down, so in a down answer the name is read bottom to top

blocks.note: Eric is a man's name

explanation.surface: A man tipped over to make a shiny finish.
explanation.definitionFit: Ciré is a fabric finish given a glossy, waxed sheen by heat and wax.

clue.text: Takes off bunged-up sounding aristocrats?

indicators.note: spoken by someone with a blocked nose, so the sound is distorted from the usual

blocks.note: toffs are posh people; with a heavy cold the first sound thickens

explanation.surface: Upper-class people with streaming colds removing their hats.
explanation.walkthrough: Toff is British slang for an upper-class person; said through a blocked nose the T comes out as D.
explanation.definitionFit: To doff a hat or garment is to remove it, a polite old word for taking off.

clue.text: Pollsters flanked by a dexter and a sinister (in these terms)

definitions.note: an adverbial phrase for an adjective: dexter and sinister are heraldic terms

indicators.note: flanked means having something on each side, so the pollsters sit between the two outer pieces

blocks.note: a plus R for right, dexter being the heraldic right
MORI is a British opinion polling company
a plus L for left, sinister being the heraldic left

explanation.surface: Opinion pollsters standing between a right-winger and a left-winger.
explanation.walkthrough: Dexter and sinister are the right and left sides of a coat of arms, so the definition points back at the clue's own words.
explanation.definitionFit: Armorial means relating to heraldry and coats of arms, whose vocabulary includes dexter and sinister.
